notes.meaning: God commands Israel never to offer an animal for sacrifice that is sick, blind, or deformed. An animal with flaws had little market value, so giving it to God cost the owner almost nothing. Offerings brought to God had to be whole and sound, pointing forward to the flawless sacrifice of Christ.

Moses warns the people against the grave sin of idolatry, whether committed by a man or a woman. Breaking God's covenant meant turning away from the Lord to worship false gods or created things like the sun, moon, and stars. God strictly forbade giving to the works of His creation the honor that belongs only to Him.

Israelite leaders could not act on mere gossip or unproven rumors. They had to investigate the report thoroughly and make sure the charge of idolatry was undeniably true. Once proven guilty, the offender was led outside the town gates and put to death by stoning in full view of the community.

A person could only be sentenced to death on the testimony of two or three credible witnesses. Capital punishment was strictly forbidden if there was only one witness. This rule protected innocent people from being condemned through personal grudges, misunderstanding, or malice.

The witnesses were required to throw the first stones, and then the rest of the community joined in. This requirement forced witnesses to search their consciences, since they had to take direct personal responsibility for an execution. Carrying out the sentence purged the contamination of evil from the community.

When local judges faced legal disputes too complex to resolve—such as hard questions of murder, property rights, or assault—they had to bring the case to the central sanctuary. There, the Levitical priests and the chief judge served as a supreme court of appeal. These leaders examined the facts under God's law and issued a final verdict.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentators have historically seen the judge here as the high priest, who served as God's chief vicar on earth to decide both religious and civil questions.

notes.meaning: The local magistrates and the disputing parties had to carry out the higher court's ruling completely. They were not permitted to alter the verdict or turn aside to the right or to the left from what was decided. Accepting this decision brought an orderly end to strife and kept the nation united under God's law.

Anyone who stubbornly refused to accept the final ruling of the priest or judge was to be put to death. Openly defying God's highest court was treated as treason against God's government. This severe punishment warned the rest of Israel so that no one would act in such pride again.

Moses looks ahead to when Israel would settle in the land and ask for a king like the surrounding nations. Even if they asked, they could not choose just anyone; they had to crown the leader God Himself selected. The king also had to be a fellow Israelite, never a foreigner who might lead the nation into idolatry.

differ.view: Rulers are placed under God's law rather than above it, providing the foundation for constitutional government where the law governs the king.

notes.meaning: The king was forbidden to build up large stables of horses or send people to Egypt to purchase them. Egypt was famous for its war chariots, and amassing them would tempt the king to trust in military force rather than in God. Returning there for commerce also risked pulling Israel back toward the pagan ways of the land that had enslaved them.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic commentators interpret this verse as specifically forbidding military alliances with Egypt to secure cavalry, rather than an invasion or physical relocation.

notes.meaning: An Israelite ruler was warned not to marry many wives, because royal harems and foreign marriage treaties would turn his heart away from the Lord. He was also forbidden to hoard excessive silver and gold for personal glory. Piling up riches and wives would lead to pride and ruin, as King Solomon later demonstrated.

Upon taking the throne, the king had to write out his own personal copy of God's law, copied from the scroll kept by the Levitical priests. This scroll was to remain with him, and he was required to read from it every day of his life. Daily study taught him to revere the Lord and keep his government aligned with God's commands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek translation of the phrase for 'a copy of this law' gave rise to the title Deuteronomy, which literally means 'second law' or repetition of the law.

notes.meaning: Daily reading of God's word kept the king humble, reminding him that he was an ordinary brother to his fellow citizens and not an absolute tyrant above them. By keeping God's commandments without turning aside, he and his sons would enjoy a long and stable reign. Godly leadership meant walking in obedience alongside his people.
